title: Peace on the messengers
hookLine: glory to your Lord, peace on the messengers, praise to Allah (37:180–182)

lines: THREE LINES TO CLOSE A GATHERING.
cards: Some songs have a refrain you start waiting for. The verse changes, the story moves on, and then the chorus comes back, and you can almost sing it before it arrives. Surah As-Saffat has one.
After several of its prophets' stories, the same short line returns: peace be on him.
And at the very end, the refrain opens up to include every messenger at once, and the surah closes with three lines some Muslims use to close a gathering.

teach.h: PEACE ON NUH, IBRAHIM, MUSA, ILYAS.
teach.b: Listen back through As-Saffat. After Nuh's story: peace be on Nuh among the worlds. After Ibrahim's: peace be on Ibrahim.
After Musa and Harun's: peace be on Musa and Harun. After Ilyas: peace be on Il-yasin. Each time, the Arabic begins salamun 'ala, peace upon.
Four of the stories end that way, in peace, however hard they were. Then the surah's last three verses.
First: glory to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe. In the verse, that clears away every wrong picture of Allah.

Then, Pickthall: "And peace be unto those sent (to warn). And praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds!" Now the refrain isn't for one prophet. It's for all of them, the named and the unnamed, everyone ever sent.

teach.h: PRAISE TO THE LORD OF THE WORLDS.
teach.b: And the last words go back to the opening of al-Fatiha: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi'l-'alamin, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. Three moves: glory, peace, praise. Glory says what Allah is above.
Peace blesses those who carried His message. Praise says where everything belongs.
Commentators, including Ibn Kathir, mention an early saying that whoever wants their reward measured out in full should end their gathering with these verses; its chain is discussed.
Some Muslims recite them at the end of a lesson, a dinner, a meeting. Wishing peace on every messenger who ever lived is not a bad way to leave a room.

how: Many Muslims recite the last three verses of As-Saffat (37:180–182) to close a lesson, a gathering or a prayer, and send peace on the prophets whenever they are named.

o: a greeting said only at the very end of prayer
peace upon: the refrain after the prophets' stories
a promise of safety for all who hear the verse

games.q: the end of As-Saffat — tap the pairs.
p: to the Lord of the Worlds

s: As-Saffat wishes peace on only one prophet
it repeats peace on Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Harun, Ilyas, then all the messengers.
the surah's last line echoes the opening of al-Fatiha
praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.
Ibn Kathir mentions an early saying about ending gatherings with these verses
its chain is discussed; some Muslims close gatherings this way.

games.q: all through As-Saffat, peace is wished on one prophet at a time. at the very end, who does the refrain include?
games.why: all the messengers, named and unnamed, between glory to Allah and praise to the Lord of the Worlds.

practice: On one breath, think glory: the verse says God is beyond whatever is pictured.
On the next, think peace, on every messenger, everyone who carried something true to people who didn't want it; on the next, praise, where everything belongs.
If you pray, you can say the three verses in Arabic or in your own language.

wordCard.voice: Salamun, peace, the refrain that follows each prophet's story in As-Saffat, and widens at the end to bless every messenger. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: and peace be on the messengers (37:181).

carryVoice: Your line: glory, peace, praise. The refrain, opened wide at the end. Day five hundred fifty-four, done.

sources.q: And peace be unto those sent (to warn). And praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds!

sources.ref: Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 37:180–182 (ending a gathering with these verses)
